studies.Screening Record ID: 20681011|Processed meat intake|Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder
studies.Population: NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study participants aged 50-71 years
studies.Ethnicity Basis: Default: no protocol-mapped specific country or population was established
studies.Ethnicity Supporting Text: Those in the highest quintile of red meat compared to those in the lowest were more likely to be non-Hispanic white
studies.Reference: Meat and components of meat and the risk of bladder cancer in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study.
studies.Authors: Ferrucci LM, Sinha R, Ward MH, Graubard BI, Hollenbeck AR, Kilfoy BA, Schatzkin A, Michaud DS, Cross AJ
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: At baseline, participants completed a 124-item food frequency questionnaire (FFQ), based on the National Cancer Institute’s Diet History Questionnaire

sample_size.excerpt: During 7 years of follow-up, 854 transitional cell bladder cancer cases were identified among 300,933 men and women who completed a validated food frequency questionnaire in the large prospective NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study.

cases.excerpt: During 1,922,817 person-years of follow-up, we identified 854 transitional cell bladder cancers (720 men, 134 women).

effect_size.excerpt: There was also no evidence of effect modification for the meat exposures by gender, smoking, or beverage intake (data not shown). We saw no clear association for total dietary nitrate (HR=0.80, 95% CI=0.58–1.10, p-trend=0.28).

comparison.excerpt: Distribution and HRs with 95% CIs for bladder cancer risk within quintiles of meat (g/1000 kcal).

design.excerpt: large prospective NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study

timing.excerpt: Follow-up for this analysis was from the date the RFQ was received until December 31, 2003, or when the participant moved out of one of the state cancer registry areas, had a cancer diagnosis, or died, whichever came first.
timing.location: Methods, Identification of cases and cohort follow-up, paragraph 2

continent.excerpt: From 1995 to 1996, the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study enrolled men and women, ages 50 to 71 years, from six U.S. states (California, Florida, Louisiana, New Jersey, North Carolina, Pennsylvania) and two metropolitan areas (Atlanta, Georgia; Detroit, Michigan).

ethnicity.excerpt: Those in the highest quintile of red meat compared to those in the lowest were more likely to be non-Hispanic white

exposure_measurement.excerpt: At baseline, participants completed a 124-item food frequency questionnaire (FFQ), based on the National Cancer Institute’s Diet History Questionnaire

gender.excerpt: Our analytic cohort consisted of 300,933 persons; 125,574 women and 175,359 men.

smoking_status.excerpt: Multivariate models were adjusted for the following characteristics which altered the risk estimates by 10% or greater: age (continuous, years), gender, smoking (never, quit ≥ 10 years ago, quit 5–9 years ago, quit 1–4 years ago, quit <1 year ago or ≤ 20 cigarettes/day, 20–40 cigarettes/day, >40 cigarettes/day)
